analysis.one_liner: Imposes a minimum tax on foreign and foreign-owned corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on April 29, 1992 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where no further action was taken before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993; it never received a committee hearing or a floor vote and died when the Congress adjourned.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new minimum tax on foreign and foreign-owned corporations. Corporations with at least 25 percent foreign ownership and foreign corporations doing business in the United States would owe an additional tax based on a percentage of their gross receipts from sales of manufactured property, with credit for regular corporate income tax already paid. The stated goal is to make sure foreign-controlled corporations doing business in America pay a baseline amount of tax rather than avoiding U.S. taxes through foreign ownership structures.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. taxpayers generally, who would benefit from the additional federal revenue, and U.S.-owned domestic corporations, which would no longer face a competitive disadvantage relative to foreign-owned rivals that can shift income abroad to avoid U.S. tax.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a floor tax so foreign-owned and foreign corporations doing business in the U.S. cannot reduce their U.S. tax liability to near zero through transfer pricing and income shifting, which ordinary taxpayers and purely domestic companies effectively help subsidize through higher deficits or higher competitive pressure.
The tax applies on top of existing taxes, so a corporation cannot escape it by exploiting deductions, deferrals, or treaties that currently reduce regular corporate tax.
Using gross receipts as the base, rather than reported income, closes off the common avoidance route of manipulating reported profit.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign-controlled domestic corporations and foreign corporations operating in the United States, which would owe the new minimum tax; to the extent these firms raise prices or reduce investment in response, U.S. consumers and workers could bear some of the cost indirectly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Foreign-owned corporations operating in the U.S.

drawbacks.text: The tax is based on gross receipts rather than income, which means low-margin or genuinely unprofitable foreign-owned businesses could owe tax even with no profit — a heavier burden than income-based taxes and potentially a disincentive to U.S. operations.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never advanced, so it received no scrutiny of its revenue estimate, economic effects, or administrative feasibility.
Targeting foreign ownership specifically could invite retaliation from trading partners against U.S. firms operating abroad, an issue commonly raised with such proposals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — requiring foreign-controlled companies to pay a baseline U.S. tax — is real and addresses a genuine fairness gap, but the gross-receipts base is a blunt instrument that could hit unprofitable businesses, and the bill never got the committee analysis that would have shown how much revenue it would raise or what the competitive side effects would be.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and died there when the 102nd Congress ended without any hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Duncan Hunter (R-CA) introduced the bill on April 29, 1992.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action was recorded; the bill never left the committee and received no vote in either chamber before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign-controlled and foreign corporations doing business in the United States are better off, since the minimum tax never took effect and they continue to owe only what regular corporate law and avoidance strategies allow. Taxpayers generally gained nothing, but also paid nothing new.

for.name: Rep. Duncan Hunter (R-CA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means; the bill had no cosponsors, so no other members publicly backed it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so there is no vote record or cosponsorship pattern from which to judge partisan alignment.

industries.industry: Foreign-controlled and foreign corporations operating in the U.S.
industries.note: The bill would have imposed a new minimum tax on these firms, reducing their ability to avoid U.S. tax through foreign ownership structures and income shifting.
Would have gained a more level competitive field against foreign-owned rivals that can shift income abroad; the bill never advanced, so no change occurred.
